sentences.text: Achillobator was a large, heavily built, bipedal carnivore measuring approximately 4.5 to 5 meters in length and weighing between 250 and 300 kilograms. This deep-bodied animal possessed relatively short arms and stocky, robust legs, featuring an unusually robust skeleton with a deep maxilla, deep femur, and a primitive pelvis with a vertically oriented pubis. It likely hunted large prey using an enlarged sickle-shaped claw on each second toe.
Although the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — lacks feather traces, evidence from related species suggests Achillobator likely had plumage.

The first remains of Achillobator were discovered in 1989 during a Mongolian-Soviet field expedition and formally described in 1999. The species was named by Altangerel Perle, Mark A. Norell, and James M. Clark.

Achillobator's stocky build and short leg ratio indicate it was not adapted for high-speed running, yet research by Perle and colleagues in 1999 suggested it had massive thighs and robust legs adapted for moderate fast-running.

Achillobator is classified within the subfamily Eudromaeosauria, a group of primarily terrestrial, hypercarnivorous dromaeosaurids. Cladistic analyses often place Achillobator as a close relative of Dromaeosaurus and Utahraptor, frequently identifying it as the sister taxon to Utahraptor.

Achillobator lived during the late Cretaceous, between approximately 93 and 80 million years ago, in what is now Asia. The type locality, Burkhant, has been identified as an Upper Cretaceous-boundary locality. Recent calcite U-Pb analyses by Kurudama and colleagues in 2020 confirmed the age of the Bayan Shireh Formation from 95.9 ± 6.0 to 89.6 ± 4.0 million years ago. The environment inhabited by Achillobator in the Bayan Shireh Formation was relatively humid, featuring extensive river and lake systems dominated by meanders, rivers, lakes, and streams.

Burnham and colleagues (2000) hypothesized that the Achillobator holotype is a paleontological chimera where only the foot claws belong to a dromaeosaurid. Researchers support the assignment of all holotype remains to a single individual because they were found in semiarticulation and share consistent color and preservation quality. Some studies, including those by Currie and Evans (2019) and Jasinski et al. (2020), place Achillobator within the subfamily Velociraptorinae.
